drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here is your opening item. An account manager uses a Claude Project to draft client proposals.
drills.scenario: Account manager, proposals miss a new tier
drills.stem: An account manager's Project drafts client proposals. Its instructions are unchanged and the service catalogue was uploaded to its knowledge in January. In March the company launched a premium support tier, announced on the intranet. Since then, proposals never mention it. What should she do?

options.A: Switch the Project to a more capable model
options.B: Replace the catalogue in the Project's knowledge with the current version, then test a proposal
options.C: Add "always include our newest services" to the Project instructions
options.D: Stop using the Project and write proposals by hand

drills.why: The trigger was the launch, so fix the part it touched. C asks for a document Claude was never given; A reads the same old file; D abandons a working setup.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. For each symptom, choose the fix
drills.prompt: Fix: examples, restrict to supplied documents and allow "I don't know", or audience and purpose? 1. Status report layout changes weekly. 2. Contract summary cites a clause not in the contract. 3. Board briefing reads like an engineering note. 4. Reply drafts structured 3 ways across the team.
drills.answer: 1 examples. 2 restrict and allow "I don't know". 3 audience and purpose. 4 examples.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A customer service team lead keeps a saved prompt
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. A removes the cause
drills.stem: Choose two. Two months ago someone added "never mention refunds unless the customer insists" to a saved complaint-reply prompt. Reviewers now say replies are evasive and never offer refunds that policy allows. Which two actions?

options.A: Rewrite the instruction with both sides: offer the refund when policy allows, explain why when not
options.B: Test the revised prompt on past complaints, including ones it handled well
options.E: Have reviewers rewrite every reply by hand from now on

drills.why: A removes the one-sided rule, B proves the fix without breaking anything. E is a compensating control dressed as a fix; C patches the patch; D is a bigger model for an instruction problem.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Every Monday an operations lead spends forty minutes
drills.stem: Every Monday an operations lead spends 40 minutes pasting the same long prompt and 3 reference files into a new chat for a supplier report. Colleagues who cover get different results. What is the best optimisation?

options.A: A Project with her tested prompt as instructions and the 3 files as knowledge, shared with cover colleagues
options.B: Keep one long chat running for every week's report
options.C: Move to the most capable model
options.D: Go back to writing the report by hand

drills.why: A removes the retyping and gives everyone the same setup. B piles up history; C doesn't explain why colleagues differ; D discards a working process.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: One more, quickly. Pause here and answer before we go on. A marketing team produces
drills.stem: A marketing team writes 200 short product descriptions a week from spec sheets, and one strategy analysis a quarter. Which setup balances quality, speed and cost?

options.A: The most capable model for both
options.B: A faster, lower-cost model for descriptions; the most capable for the strategy analysis

drills.why: Match each task to its needs. A overspends on routine work, C underpowers the reasoning, D adds web lookups the spec sheets don't need.

drills.question_line: SAM: Your turn. Pause and name the three objectives
drills.prompt: Name the three objectives, and the first question each one asks.
drills.answer: Diagnosis: what changed? Feedback: what exactly is wrong, and did the fix break anything? Optimisation: where is time or money going on work that doesn't need it?

In this episode: Find the cause of a poor output by asking what changed
Match common symptoms to their fixes
Turn vague feedback into a tested change
Streamline a weekly workflow without overspending
Cold open: the missing tier: First question: what changed, or what is missing?
Check: request, material, setup, conversation, the task itself
Instructions can't add capability: calculations need something that computes
Generic: specifics. Off-topic: the real goal. Format drift: examples
Invented details: allow "I don't know", restrict to supplied documents
Adjusting to feedback: Turn vague feedback into a specific instruction with a reason
Ask the reviewer for one example of good
A patch for every complaint makes rules fight
Old defensive rules cause deflection; note why each was added
State both sides of any cost you ask Claude to weigh
Test changes on past cases, including ones that worked
Optimising the workflow: Efficiency and effectiveness: fewer minutes, less rework
Match the model to the work
Long chat drifted: summarise the decisions, start fresh
Measure before and after on the same measure
Human review where the stakes need it
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: B, replace the catalogue, then test
Claude only sees the January catalogue
An instruction can't supply a missing document
A bigger model reads the same old file
Five to remember: Diagnose first: what changed? Request, material, setup, conversation, task
Symptom to fix: format, examples; invented, restrict; register, audience
Instructions can't add knowledge or capability
Specific feedback with a reason; remove old or one-sided rules; regression-test
Projects for tested prompts, model matched to work, restart long chats
Recap: the exam tells: A named change and a start date → the part that change touched
Told to use information it doesn't have → instructions can't add knowledge
Vague feedback → a specific, checkable instruction with a reason
Evasive or over-cautious → an old or one-sided rule
Same prompt retyped, colleagues differ → a shared Project
High volume, routine → a faster, lower-cost model
Long chat drifted → summarise and restart
